content: Hereditary ataxia syndromes, including Friedreich ataxia, often lead to significant speech impairments, most commonly dysarthria. Dysarthria refers to a group of motor speech disorders caused by impaired muscular control, which can severely affect an individual's ability to communicate and participate in social activities, ultimately reducing their quality of life. Addressing speech impairments in these conditions is crucial, and evidence-based treatments are necessary. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of interventions for speech disorders in adults and children with Friedreich ataxia and other hereditary ataxias. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared treatments for hereditary ataxias with no treatment, placebo, or other interventions, focusing on speech production outcomes. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and trial registries up to October 2013. Fourteen clinical trials involving 721 participants met the inclusion criteria. Thirteen of these trials investigated pharmaceutical treatments compared to placebo or low-dose interventions in heterogeneous groups of individuals with degenerative cerebellar ataxias. The pharmaceutical agents studied included L-5HT (levorotatory form of 5-hydroxytryptophan), idebenone, thyrotropin-releasing hormone tartrate (TRH-T), riluzole, varenicline, buspirone, betamethasone, coenzyme Q10 with vitamin E, α-tocopheryl quinone, and erythropoietin. Each of these compounds was studied in one trial, except for L-5HT, idebenone, and TRH-T, which were each studied in two trials. The 14th trial evaluated the effectiveness of nonspecific physiotherapy and occupational therapy in an inpatient setting compared to no treatment. Notably, none of the studies utilized traditional speech therapy approaches. The primary outcome measure for the review was defined as the percentage improvement in overall speech production immediately after the intervention or at a later time, assessed using validated speech assessment tools. However, none of the trials included speech as a primary outcome or used validated tools to measure speech. Instead, eleven studies reported speech outcomes derived from subscales embedded within broader disease rating scales. Three studies used alternative methods to assess speech, such as measuring the mean time to produce a standard sentence, subjective ratings on a 14-point scale, patient-reported impacts of dysarthria on daily activities, and acoustic measures of syllable length. One study combined subjective disease rating scale assessments with additional speech timing measures. Five studies reported statistically significant improvements in overall disease severity on scales that included speech subscales. However, only three of these studies provided specific data on speech performance, all of which were comparisons with placebo. Improvements in overall disease severity were observed with α-tocopheryl quinone, but no significant changes were noted on the speech subscale in individuals with Friedreich ataxia. Betamethasone showed a statistically significant improvement in speech according to a speech disorders subscale. Riluzole demonstrated a statistically significant effect on speech in participants with mixed hereditary, sporadic, and unknown origin ataxias. No other pharmaceutical interventions showed significant differences in speech outcomes compared to placebo. The rehabilitation study reported a statistically significant improvement in functional independence at the end of the treatment period compared to the delayed treatment group. However, these effects were not sustained 12 to 24 weeks after treatment. None of the four studies assessing quality of life found significant effects. Adverse events were reported for 13 pharmaceutical therapies, with minor side effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms and nausea being the most common. Serious adverse events were reported in two participants in one of the L-5HT trials (leading to discontinuation due to gastrointestinal effects) and in four participants in the idebenone studies (three taking idebenone and one taking placebo). Serious adverse events with idebenone included gastrointestinal side effects, chest pain, and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura in individuals with a prior history of these conditions. The rehabilitation study did not report any adverse events. The review identified several methodological limitations in the included studies. Six studies were considered to have a high risk of bias, with issues such as inadequate blinding of participants or assessors in four studies, poor randomization in two studies, reporting bias in two studies, and attrition bias in four studies. Only one study was judged to have a low risk of bias across all criteria. Additionally, the validity of the measurement scales used in the studies was questioned, leading to a downgrading of the quality of evidence for many outcomes to low or very low. In conclusion, there is insufficient and lowor very low-quality evidence from RCTs or observational studies to determine the effectiveness of any treatment for speech disorders in hereditary ataxia syndromes. Further high-quality research is needed to establish effective interventions for these conditions.
